question: What is an Azure Virtual Network (VNet), and how does it relate to the PaaS services you've been using (Logic Apps, Function Apps, API Management, Service Bus)?
answer_html:
A Virtual Network (VNet) is an isolated, private network you define inside Azure. It's the logical equivalent of a physical network in a traditional datacenter: you pick an IP address range for it, and everything you place inside can talk to everything else inside using private IP addresses, invisible from the public internet.

When you've used Logic Apps, Function Apps, or API Management, Azure was silently running a VNet-equivalent for you behind the scenes, or your traffic was going out over the public internet edge of those services. Integration features like VNet Integration for Function Apps, or Private Endpoints for Service Bus and Key Vault, are exactly the seam between the PaaS layer you know and the infrastructure layer you're now learning: they plug a managed service into a VNet you control, instead of leaving it fully public.

A VNet is defined with a CIDR block, for example 10.0.0.0/16, giving you roughly 65,000 private addresses to carve up. It doesn't do anything by itself — it's a container. The real work happens in the subnets, NSGs, and routes inside it, which the next few questions cover.

question: What is a subnet, and why do engineers split a VNet into multiple subnets instead of using one flat address space?
answer_html:
A subnet is a subdivision of a VNet's address range. If your VNet is 10.0.0.0/16, you might carve out 10.0.1.0/24 for web servers, 10.0.2.0/24 for a database tier, and 10.0.3.0/27 for a small set of management VMs. Every resource you deploy into the VNet — a VM, an Application Gateway, a VNet-integrated Function App — lives inside exactly one subnet.

Subnets exist for two practical reasons:

  • Security boundaries. Network Security Groups (covered next) are typically attached at the subnet level, so putting your database tier in its own subnet lets you write one rule set that applies to everything there, separate from the rules for your web tier.
  • Routing and delegation. Some Azure services require a dedicated, delegated subnet to inject themselves into your network — Azure Firewall, VPN Gateway, and Function App VNet Integration all reserve a subnet just for themselves. You can't mix general-purpose VMs into a delegated subnet.

Azure also reserves 5 IP addresses in every subnet for its own use (network address, gateway, DNS, and two more), so a /24 subnet gives you 251 usable addresses, not 256. This trips people up when sizing subnets for the first time.

question: What is a Network Security Group (NSG), and what does it actually control?
answer_html:
A Network Security Group (NSG) is a stateful, distributed firewall you attach to a subnet or to a specific network interface. It's a list of allow/deny rules evaluated against traffic entering (inbound) or leaving (outbound) that subnet or NIC. Conceptually it's the closest infra-layer analog to the access policies you already write for API Management or Key Vault firewall rules — except NSGs operate at the IP/port level (layer 3/4), not at the HTTP/application level.

Each rule has: a priority number, a source, a destination, a protocol (TCP/UDP/*), a port range, and an allow or deny action. A typical rule might allow inbound TCP on port 443 from Internet to a web subnet, or deny all inbound traffic from anywhere by default.

Two things matter that are easy to miss coming from PaaS:

  • NSGs are stateful — if you allow an inbound request, the matching response traffic is automatically allowed back out; you don't need a mirrored outbound rule.
  • Every subnet and NIC has a set of platform default rules already present (allow VNet-to-VNet traffic, allow Azure Load Balancer probes, deny everything else from the internet) that exist even before you add a single rule of your own.

question: You've never designed network topology, only consumed managed services behind it. What's the mental model shift from PaaS to infra-level Azure networking?
answer_html:
The core shift is: in PaaS, Azure hides the network and you configure access (connection strings, firewall allow-lists, managed identities). At the infra layer, you build the network, and access is a side effect of topology — what subnet something sits in, what route table applies to it, what NSG governs it, and what DNS zone resolves its name.

A useful way to translate concepts you already know:

  • API Management's IP allow-list → is the App-layer equivalent of an NSG rule at layer 3/4.
  • Service Bus's “Selected networks” firewall → is a coarse version of what a Service Endpoint or Private Endpoint does properly (question 7 goes deep on this).
  • A Function App's outbound IP addresses being unpredictable on the Consumption plan → is exactly the problem VNet Integration solves, by giving the function a private, predictable path into a VNet you control.

From here on, every answer builds on three primitives you now know: the VNet (the container), the subnet (the placement unit), and the NSG (the traffic filter). Routing, peering, load balancing, and hybrid connectivity are all just more sophisticated things layered on top of those three.

question: How does Azure evaluate NSG rules, and what determines which rule wins when two rules could both apply to the same traffic?
answer_html:
Every NSG rule has a priority, a number between 100 and 4096. Azure evaluates rules in ascending priority order — lowest number first — and stops at the first rule that matches the traffic's source, destination, port, and protocol. Whatever that first matching rule says (allow or deny) is final; no other rule is consulted afterward, no matter how specific it might be.

This means rule order matters more than rule specificity. A broad deny all inbound, priority 100 rule will silently swallow a very precise allow port 443 from a single IP, priority 200 rule, because 100 is evaluated first and already produced a match. This is the single most common “my NSG rule isn't working” bug in real environments.

Also remember there are two separate rule sets, evaluated independently:

  • Inbound rules control traffic arriving at the subnet/NIC.
  • Outbound rules control traffic leaving it.

And if an NSG is attached at both the subnet and the NIC, traffic must pass both NSGs' evaluation — a deny at either layer blocks it, regardless of what the other allows.

question: What is VNet peering, and what are its key constraints (non-transitivity, address space, name resolution)?
answer_html:
VNet peering connects two VNets so resources in each can reach each other over private IP addresses, using Microsoft's backbone rather than the public internet. Once peered, there's no gateway or extra hop — traffic between the VNets is essentially as fast as traffic within one VNet.

The constraint that catches people out most is that peering is not transitive. If VNet A is peered with VNet B, and VNet B is peered with VNet C, resources in A cannot reach resources in C through B. Each pair that needs connectivity must be explicitly peered, or routed through a shared hub (see the hub-and-spoke question later).

Other things to know:

  • Peered VNets must have non-overlapping address spaces. If both use 10.0.0.0/16, they can never be peered — this is why address planning across an organization matters from day one.
  • Peering is configured as two link objects, one from each VNet's side, and both must be established for traffic to flow.
  • By default, peering does not automatically share private DNS zone resolution between the VNets — that has to be linked separately (see the DNS question), so two peered VNets might have connectivity but still fail to resolve each other's private names.

question: What's the difference between a Private Endpoint and a Service Endpoint for a service like Service Bus or Key Vault, and when would you pick one over the other?
answer_html:
Both features exist to let a VNet reach an Azure PaaS service (Service Bus, Key Vault, Storage, SQL, etc.) without that traffic crossing the public internet — but they work in fundamentally different ways.

A Service Endpoint is a routing optimization: it tells the subnet to send traffic destined for a given service (e.g. all of Azure Storage) directly over the Azure backbone instead of out through the public internet path. The service still has a public IP address and endpoint; the Service Endpoint just changes the route and lets the service's firewall recognize traffic as coming from your VNet/subnet, so you can lock it down to “selected networks.” This is the closest thing to what you may have used as the “Selected networks” firewall option on Service Bus or Key Vault.

A Private Endpoint goes further: it provisions an actual private IP address inside your subnet that maps directly to that specific PaaS resource instance, using Azure Private Link. The service effectively gets a network interface inside your VNet. Traffic never touches a public IP at all, and you can fully disable the service's public endpoint. This is why Private Endpoint is the modern default recommendation for anything security-sensitive.

Practical rule of thumb: Private Endpoint when you need the resource to disappear from the public internet entirely and be addressable by a private IP (works across peered VNets and on-prem via VPN/ExpressRoute too); Service Endpoint when you just want cheaper, faster, backbone routing plus a coarse network-based allow-list, and don't need full public-access removal.

question: How do you choose between Azure Load Balancer, Application Gateway, and Front Door?
answer_html:
All three distribute traffic across multiple backend instances, but they operate at different layers and different scopes, which is what actually drives the choice.

  • Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP). It doesn't look inside the request at all — it just spreads connections across backend VMs or instances based on IP/port. Use it for raw throughput, non-HTTP protocols, or when you don't need routing decisions based on URL path or headers. It comes in public and internal (private-IP-only) flavors, and it's regional.
  • Application Gateway works at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). It can route based on URL path or hostname, do TLS termination, and includes an optional Web Application Firewall (WAF) mode for OWASP-style protections. It's still a regional service — it lives inside one VNet/subnet and load-balances across backends within that region.
  • Front Door is also layer 7, but it's a global, edge-based service. It terminates connections at Microsoft's edge points-of-presence close to the user, then routes to the closest/healthiest backend region, and can also do WAF, caching, and SSL offload. Use it when you have backends in multiple regions and want global load balancing, low-latency edge termination, or CDN-style caching in front of them.

A common real-world stack layers these: Front Door at the global edge, routing into a regional Application Gateway (for WAF and path-based routing), which in turn sits in front of a Load Balancer or the app tier directly.

question: What is a User-Defined Route (UDR), and why would you need one if VNets already route traffic automatically?
answer_html:
Azure creates system routes automatically for every subnet: routes to other subnets in the same VNet, routes to peered VNets, a default route to the internet, and so on. Most of the time these are exactly what you want, and you never have to think about routing at all — another reason the network layer stays invisible from PaaS.

A User-Defined Route (UDR) is a manual override you attach to a subnet via a route table, when you need traffic to take a path that isn't the default. The most common reason is forcing traffic through a network appliance for inspection — for example, a route that says “anything destined for 0.0.0.0/0 (the internet), send it to the private IP of our Azure Firewall or NVA instead of straight out,” so all egress gets inspected before leaving. This pattern is often called forced tunneling.

Other reasons include routing traffic from a spoke VNet through a hub before reaching another spoke (since peering isn't transitive), or routing around a specific subnet during a migration.

Key mechanics: a route table is created as its own resource, associated to one or more subnets, and contains routes with an address prefix and a next hop type — Virtual Appliance (an IP address), VirtualNetworkGateway, VNetPeering, Internet, or None (black-hole the traffic). When both a UDR and a system route could apply, the more specific prefix wins, and a UDR with an equally specific prefix overrides the system route.

question: What are the trade-offs between VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute for connecting an on-premises network to Azure, and how would you decide which one a given workload needs?
answer_html:
Both connect an on-premises network to a VNet, but they differ in path, guarantees, and cost, which is exactly what should drive the decision.

  • VPN Gateway creates an encrypted IPsec tunnel over the public internet. It's quick to provision, cheap, and fine for moderate throughput (a site-to-site VPN Gateway tops out roughly in the 1–10 Gbps range depending on SKU). Because it rides the public internet, latency and throughput are not guaranteed — you're subject to normal internet congestion and variability.
  • ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated circuit from your on-premises network to Microsoft's network, provisioned through a connectivity provider, never touching the public internet. It offers predictable latency, higher throughput (circuits up to 100 Gbps with ExpressRoute Direct), and an SLA on the connection itself. It costs significantly more and takes longer to provision, since it involves a physical circuit.

The deciding factors in an interview-style scenario: if the requirement mentions guaranteed low latency, high sustained throughput, or compliance requirements that traffic never cross the public internet (e.g. large data migrations, real-time trading, hybrid SAP workloads) — that's ExpressRoute. If it's a smaller branch office, a dev/test hybrid link, or a budget-constrained scenario where occasional latency variance is acceptable, VPN Gateway is the right call. In practice, many enterprises run both: ExpressRoute as primary, with a VPN Gateway as an automatic failover path if the circuit goes down.

question: Two VNets are peered, but VMs in each still can't reach each other. Walk through how you'd diagnose this using Network Watcher, effective routes, and NSG flow logs.
answer_html:
This is a classic layered problem — peering being “Connected” only proves the control-plane link exists, not that traffic actually flows. Work through the stack methodically:

  • Confirm the peering state itself. Both sides must show Connected; a one-sided or failed peering means no traffic moves regardless of anything else.
  • Check for overlapping or since-changed address spaces. Peering silently stops working if either VNet's address space was modified after the peering was created without re-syncing.
  • Use Network Watcher's IP flow verify to test, from a specific VM, whether a given source/destination/port/protocol combination is allowed or denied, and by which rule and NSG. This directly answers “is an NSG blocking this?” without manually re-deriving rule priority by hand.
  • Pull effective routes on the VM's NIC. This shows the actual merged routing table Azure is using — system routes plus any UDRs — and will reveal if a route table on one side is sending return traffic somewhere other than back through the peering (a very common cause: a UDR intended for internet egress accidentally black-holing or redirecting peered-VNet traffic too).
  • Pull effective NSG rules on the NIC, which merges subnet-level and NIC-level NSGs into the single rule set actually being applied, so you're not checking the two NSGs separately and missing an interaction.
  • Turn on NSG flow logs (via Network Watcher) if the above isn't conclusive, to see actual accepted/denied flow records over time — useful when the failure is intermittent or asymmetric rather than a flat block.

In practice, the two most common root causes are an NSG deny rule with a lower (higher-priority) number than the intended allow rule, and a UDR that was added for a different purpose (like forced tunneling) that unintentionally captures the peered VNet's address range too.

question: How would you design a hub-and-spoke network topology in Azure, and what problem is it solving?
answer_html:
Hub-and-spoke is the standard enterprise pattern for organizing multiple VNets so that shared services and security controls live in one place instead of being duplicated everywhere.

  • The hub VNet holds shared infrastructure: a VPN Gateway and/or ExpressRoute connection for on-premises connectivity, a central firewall or Network Virtual Appliance (NVA) for traffic inspection, and often shared services like DNS resolvers.
  • Each spoke VNet holds an actual workload (e.g. one spoke per application or environment), and is peered directly to the hub — but spokes are not peered to each other.
  • Because peering isn't transitive, spoke-to-spoke traffic and spoke-to-on-prem traffic must be forced through the hub. This is done with User-Defined Routes on each spoke subnet, sending 0.0.0.0/0 (or specific prefixes) to the hub firewall/NVA's private IP as the next hop, combined with the hub peering having “use remote gateway”/gateway-transit settings enabled so spokes can reach on-prem through the hub's VPN Gateway or ExpressRoute circuit.

This design solves several problems at once: on-premises connectivity is configured and paid for once, not per workload; a single firewall/NVA can enforce and log all inter-spoke and outbound traffic; and address planning stays centralized since every spoke must have a non-overlapping range from the hub and from every other spoke.

The main alternative today is Azure Virtual WAN, which is Microsoft's managed version of the same hub-and-spoke concept — it automates the hub, the routing between spokes, and branch/VPN/ExpressRoute connectivity, trading some manual control for far less operational overhead at scale.
